# Lab Exercise 6A

## Introduction

This laboratory exercise introduces statistical comparisons used to determine whether a sample differs from a reference value or whether two groups differ. The appropriate test depends on the research question, the type of data, and the study design. You will practice one-sample, paired-sample, and independent-group comparisons.

For each comparison, you will explore the data, formulate hypotheses, check assumptions, and conduct the analysis in R. You will also interpret and report the results using test statistics, p-values, confidence intervals, estimates, and visualizations.

## Practice Exercise


```{r}
library(tidyverse)
```

### 6.4.1 One-Sample Comparison: Ozone Concentration

The question is whether the mean recorded daily ozone concentration differs from 30 ppb.

#### 1a. Load and inspect the data

```{r}
data("airquality")
head(airquality)
str(airquality)
```

The dataset contains 153 daily observations and six variables. Ozone concentration is numerical, and some of its values are missing.

#### 1b. Check the summary statistics

```{r}
summary(airquality$Ozone)
```

The recorded ozone concentrations range from 1 to 168 ppb. The median is 31.5 ppb, the mean is about 42.13 ppb, and the variable contains missing values.

#### 1c. Identify available and missing measurements

```{r}
sum(is.na(airquality$Ozone))
sum(!is.na(airquality$Ozone))
```

There are 37 missing ozone measurements and 116 recorded measurements.

#### 1d–1e. Keep recorded measurements and count the observations

```{r}
ozone_data <- airquality[!is.na(airquality$Ozone), ]

table(is.na(ozone_data$Ozone))
summary(ozone_data$Ozone)
```

I kept the 116 rows with a recorded ozone concentration. No missing ozone values remain in the filtered data.

#### 2. Explore the distribution

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

ggplot(ozone_data, aes(x = Ozone)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 10, color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Daily Ozone Concentrations",
    x = "Ozone concentration (ppb)",
    y = "Number of days"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

ggplot(ozone_data, aes(x = "", y = Ozone)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Ozone Concentrations",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Ozone concentration (ppb)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The histogram is strongly right-skewed. The boxplot shows several high observations, including possible outliers.

#### 3. State the hypotheses

The null hypothesis is that the population mean daily ozone concentration is 30 ppb. The alternative hypothesis is that the population mean differs from 30 ppb. I use a two-sided test with α = 0.05.

#### 4. Assess assumptions and choose a test

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

ggplot(ozone_data, aes(sample = Ozone)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Normal Q-Q Plot of Ozone Concentrations",
    x = "Theoretical quantiles",
    y = "Ozone concentration (ppb)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

shapiro.test(ozone_data$Ozone)
```

The histogram and Q-Q plot show a strong departure from normality, and the Shapiro–Wilk test gives a p-value below 0.05. Following the decision rule in the manual, the one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test is the rank-based choice. It tests a location shift, not the arithmetic mean. Because the research question specifically asks about the mean, I also report the one-sample t-test and interpret it with caution due to the skew and high observations.

#### 5. Conduct and report the analysis

```{r}
wilcox.test(ozone_data$Ozone, mu = 30, alternative = "two.sided")
t.test(ozone_data$Ozone, mu = 30, alternative = "two.sided")
```

The Wilcoxon test indicates that the location of the recorded ozone measurements differs from 30 ppb. The one-sample t-test reports the sample mean, test statistic, p-value, and confidence interval for the population mean.

#### 6. Interpret the findings

The sample mean was about 42.13 ppb, which is higher than the reference value of 30 ppb. The one-sample t-test found a statistically significant difference, *t*(115) = 3.96, *p* < 0.001, with a 95% confidence interval of approximately 36.06 to 48.20 ppb. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test also found evidence of a difference in location (*p* < 0.05). These results indicate that recorded ozone concentrations were higher than 30 ppb in this dataset. The skewed distribution and possible time dependence should be considered when interpreting the result.

### 6.4.2 Paired Comparison: Chick Weights at Day 10 and Day 21

The question is whether mean chick body weight differs between Day 10 and Day 21 among chicks measured at both times.

#### 1. Load and inspect the data

```{r}
data("ChickWeight")
head(ChickWeight)
str(ChickWeight)
summary(ChickWeight)
```

The data contain repeated body-weight measurements for chicks assigned to different diets. This comparison uses only the Day 10 and Day 21 measurements.

#### 2a–2e. Prepare and inspect complete pairs

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

chick_wide <- ChickWeight |>
  filter(Time %in% c(10, 21)) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = Time,
    values_from = weight,
    names_prefix = "day"
  )

chick_complete <- chick_wide |>
  filter(!is.na(day10), !is.na(day21)) |>
  mutate(difference = day21 - day10)

head(chick_wide)
head(chick_complete)
chick_wide |> summarise(total_chicks = n())
chick_complete |> summarise(
  complete_pairs = n(),
  mean_difference = mean(difference),
  sd_difference = sd(difference)
)
```

I matched measurements by chick and kept only chicks with weights at both time points. There are 45 complete pairs. I calculated each difference as Day 21 weight minus Day 10 weight, so a positive difference means the chick weighed more on Day 21.

#### 3. Explore the paired differences

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

ggplot(chick_complete, aes(x = difference)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 10, color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Differences in Chick Weight",
    x = "Day 21 weight minus Day 10 weight (g)",
    y = "Number of chicks"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The differences show the direction and spread of weight changes for the same chicks. Most differences are positive, so most chicks weighed more on Day 21.

#### 4. State the hypotheses

Let the paired difference be Day 21 weight minus Day 10 weight. The null hypothesis is that the population mean difference is 0 g. The alternative hypothesis is that the population mean difference is not 0 g. I use α = 0.05.

#### 5. Assess assumptions and choose a test

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

ggplot(chick_complete, aes(sample = difference)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Normal Q-Q Plot of Paired Differences",
    x = "Theoretical quantiles",
    y = "Weight difference (g)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

shapiro.test(chick_complete$difference)
```

The normality assumption applies to the paired differences. I use the Q-Q plot and Shapiro–Wilk result together: if the p-value is below 0.05 and the plot shows a departure from the reference line, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test is preferred under the manual’s rule. Otherwise, the paired t-test is appropriate. The paired t-test directly tests the mean difference; the Wilcoxon test is rank-based.

#### 6. Conduct the tests

```{r}
t.test(chick_complete$day21, chick_complete$day10, paired = TRUE)
wilcox.test(chick_complete$day21, chick_complete$day10, paired = TRUE)
```

Both outputs are shown. I use the normality assessment above to identify the preferred test. The paired t-test directly addresses the question about the mean difference, while the Wilcoxon signed-rank test provides the rank-based alternative described in the manual.

#### 7. Interpret and report the findings

Among the 45 chicks with complete measurements, body weight increased from Day 10 to Day 21. The paired t-test output gives the estimated mean difference, test statistic, p-value, and confidence interval for that mean change. The Wilcoxon output gives the rank-based result. The normality assessment determines which test is preferred under the manual’s decision rule. Overall, the results show that the chicks in this sample were heavier on Day 21; the Wilcoxon result should be interpreted as a difference in location rather than as a direct test of the mean.

### 6.4.3 Independent-Group Comparison: PlantGrowth

The question is whether mean plant dry weight differs between the control group and treatment 1.

#### 1. Load and inspect the data

```{r}
data("PlantGrowth")
head(PlantGrowth)
str(PlantGrowth)
summary(PlantGrowth)
```

The dataset contains dry weights for plants in a control group and two treatment groups. This exercise compares the control group and treatment 1.

#### 2. Select the two groups

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

plant_two <- PlantGrowth |>
  filter(group %in% c("ctrl", "trt1")) |>
  droplevels()

table(plant_two$group)
```

The selected data contain 10 plants in each group. Each plant is in only one group, so the groups are independent.

#### 3. State the hypotheses

The null hypothesis is that the population mean plant weights are equal in the control and treatment 1 groups. The alternative hypothesis is that the population means differ. I use a two-sided test with α = 0.05.

#### 4. Explore the data

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

ggplot(plant_two, aes(x = group, y = weight)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Plant Dry Weight by Group",
    x = "Group",
    y = "Plant dry weight (g)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

plant_two |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_weight = mean(weight),
    sd_weight = sd(weight)
  )
```

The control group had a mean weight of 5.032 g, while treatment 1 had a mean weight of 4.661 g. The boxplot and standard deviations help compare the spread and identify unusual observations.

#### 5. Assess assumptions and choose a test

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

ggplot(plant_two, aes(sample = weight)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line() +
  facet_wrap(~group) +
  labs(
    title = "Normal Q-Q Plots of Plant Weight by Group",
    x = "Theoretical quantiles",
    y = "Plant dry weight (g)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

shapiro.test(plant_two$weight[plant_two$group == "ctrl"])
shapiro.test(plant_two$weight[plant_two$group == "trt1"])
```

The observations are independent and plant weight is numerical. The Q-Q plots and Shapiro–Wilk tests do not show strong evidence against normality in either group. Welch’s two-sample t-test is appropriate for comparing the means and does not require equal population variances, so I do not need a separate equal-variance test to use it.

#### 6. Conduct the test

```{r}
t.test(weight ~ group, data = plant_two)
```

The output reports Welch’s test statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, estimated group means, and confidence interval for the difference.

#### 7. Interpret and report the findings

Mean plant dry weight was 5.032 g in the control group and 4.661 g in treatment 1, an estimated difference of 0.371 g (control minus treatment 1). Welch’s two-sample t-test did not show a statistically significant difference between the group means, *t*(16.52) = 1.19, *p* = 0.250. The 95% confidence interval for the mean difference was approximately −0.288 to 1.030 g and includes zero. I fail to reject the null hypothesis because the data do not provide sufficient evidence that the population mean plant dry weights differ between the control and treatment 1 groups.
